extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, comic writers, essayists, and readers interested in character, stage conduct, and conversation
extracted.subtask_short: writing comic character and stage conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating comic characters, conversational 'butts', and morally-conscious stagecraft: how to produce laughter, avoid cheap vulgarity, portray social types realistically, and use character to instruct as well as amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of laughter: betraying oddness or infirmity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Man of Wit makes us laugh, it is by betraying some Oddness or Infirmity in his own Character, or in the Representation which he makes of others; and when we laugh at a Brute or even an inanimate thing, it is at some Action or Incident that bears a remote Analogy to any Blunder or Absurdity in reasonable Creatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter should arise from exposing a character's oddness/flaw or staging incidents that echo human blunders; comedic effect depends on analogies between actions and recognisable human absurdities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a conversational 'Butt'
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man is not qualified for a Butt, who has not a good deal of Wit and Vivacity, even in the ridiculous side of his Character. A stupid Butt is only fit for the Conversation of ordinary People: Men of Wit require one that will give them Play, and bestir himself in the absurd Part of his Behaviour. A Butt with these Accomplishments frequently gets the Laugh of his side, and turns the Ridicule upon him that attacks him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For conversational comedy, create 'butt' characters who are themselves lively and witty (even in their ridiculousness) so they provide material for sharper wits and can sometimes reverse the ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listening and flatterers as conversational technique
rubrics_metrics.description: When you fall into a Man's Conversation, the first thing you should consider is, whether he has a greater Inclination to hear you, or that you should hear him. The latter is the more general Desire, and I know very able Flatterers that never speak a Word in Praise of the Persons from whom they obtain daily Favours, but still practise a skilful Attention to whatever is uttered by those with whom they converse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray flatterers and social manipulators through their attentive silence rather than constant praise; show conversational power dynamics (who speaks vs who listens) for realism and comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using bawdy/smut as a substitute for invention
rubrics_metrics.description: No one ever writ Bawdy for any other Reason but Dearth of Invention. When the Author cannot strike out of himself any more of that which he has superior to those who make up the Bulk of his Audience, his natural Recourse is to that which he has in common with them; and a Description which gratifies a sensual Appetite will please, when the Author has nothing about him to delight a refined Imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sexual or lascivious content as an expedient symptomatic of weak invention; writers should avoid relying on 'luscious expressions' to make up for lack of wit or original material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage conduct regarding chastity and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Such an Image as [a lascivious one] ought, by no means, to be presented to a Chaste and Regular Audience... I recommend to your Consideration, as a SPECTATOR, the conduct of the Stage at present with Relation to Chastity and Modesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of the audience's moral expectations; avoid gratuitous sexual imagery and dialogue that offends modesty—stage content should consider the sensibilities of chaste audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors' gestures and actresses as crutches for weak plays
rubrics_metrics.description: It lifts an heavy empty Sentence, when there is added to it a lascivious Gesture of Body; and when it is too low to be raised even by that, a flat Meaning is enlivened by making it a double one... When a Poet flags in writing Lusciously, a pretty Girl can move Lasciviously, and have the same good Consequence for the Author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid crafting dialogue that depends on suggestive gestures or the sexual allure of performers to succeed; this is an anti-pattern—rely on stronger writing rather than bodily display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform comic outcomes: punish vice, reward virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: If Men of Wit... would turn their Thoughts upon raising it from good natural Impulses... might not such a one divert the Audience quite as well, if at the Catastrophe he were found out for a Traitor, and met with Contempt accordingly?... there is room enough to catch at Men's Hearts to their Good and Advantage, if the Poets will attempt it with the Honesty which becomes their Characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reshaping comedies so that vice leads to disgrace and virtue is honoured—comic plots can instruct as well as amuse by showing consequences rather than rewarding immoral behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character construction: combine virtue with wit
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man that is Temperate, Generous, Valiant, Chaste, Faithful and Honest, may, at the same time, have Wit, Humour, Mirth, Good-breeding, and Gallantry. While he exerts these latter Qualities, twenty Occasions might be invented to shew he is Master of the other noble Virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft protagonists who embody moral virtues while remaining entertaining; use their wit and humour to reveal, reinforce, and exemplify those virtues rather than mask vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting coffee-house/social microcosms by types and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Men differ rather in the Time of Day in which they make a Figure... I, who am at the Coffee-house at Six in a Morning, know that my Friend Beaver the Haberdasher has a Levy of more undissembled Friends and Admirers... When the Day grows too busy for these Gentlemen to enjoy any longer the Pleasures of their Deshabilé, they give place to Men who have Business or good Sense in their Faces... Of these sort of Men consist the worthier Part of Mankind... Having here given an Account of the several Reigns that succeed each other from Day-break till Dinner-time...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing social scenes, populate them with recognizable types defined by time-of-day and habits (early loungers, fashionable virtuosi, serious businessfolk, the worthies) and show how their presence shifts the tone and power dynamics of the space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ethnocentric or narrow judgments in travel/portrait writing
rubrics_metrics.description: We are all guilty in some Measure of the same narrow way of Thinking, which we meet with in this Abstract of the Indian Journal; when we fancy the Customs, Dress, and Manners of other Countries are ridiculous and extravagant, if they do not resemble those of our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In travel writing or cultural portraiture, beware of assuming foreign customs are ridiculous; practice self-awareness and avoid mocking differences simply because they diverge from one's own norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging authenticity vs false splendour
rubrics_metrics.description: They are so far from falling into these false Gallantries, that the Stage is here in its Original Situation of a Cart... tho' they have had a full Barn for many Days together, our Itinerants are still so wretchedly poor, that without you can prevail to send us the Furniture you forbid at the Play-house, the Heroes appear only like sturdy Beggars, and the Heroines Gipsies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that a lack of costly stage furniture or finery can produce authentic, sometimes comic, effects; do not assume that grand dress is always required—consider how poverty or plainness can serve the piece.
